2.text: ally tied into a loop. A short bone or ivory rod, or a long, slender piece

3.text: of iron (Fig. 34, a³), is inserted in the upper end of the shaft, where it is

4.text: held firmly with lashings. Sometimes it is also wound around with a thin

5.text: strip of leather. The upper point of the rod is inserted in a circular hole in

6.text: the slanting base of the harpoon-head, which fits it tightly (Fig. 34, a⁴). The

7.text: harpoon-head is released as soon as it strikes the game.

8.text: Frequently the rod is replaced by two separate pieces. The lower piece

9.text: (Fig. 34, b³), which is stout, and cylindrical in shape, is fastened firmly to the

10.text: shaft. The upper piece (Fig. 34, b⁴) is a slender ivory rod, with a hole in the

11.text: middle. Through the hole is passed a thin strip of leather, both ends of which

12.text: are fastened to the lashings of the ivory cylinder, forming a loop. The lower

13.text: end of the rod fits into a hole in the cylinder, and the loop, thus tightened,

14.text: holds it in place, while the harpoon-head is firmly set on its top. The whole

15.text: is at the same time tight and elastic. The head becomes disengaged with the

16.text: blow and remains in the wound, while the movable rod separates from the

17.text: cylinder and hangs down suspended by the loop.

18.text: The lower end of the shaft is furnished with a strong bone or iron point

19.text: (Fig. 34, b⁵) firmly attached by means of a strip of leather. The old method

20.text: of attachment, by passing the line through holes made with a drill (Fig. 34, b⁶),

21.text: is still employed. The point is used as an ice-pick for breaking holes through

22.text: the ice, also for testing the depth of the snow, etc. In some cases a slender

23.text: piece of ivory, used for testing thin, newly formed ice, is substituted for the

24.text: bone or iron point. The shaft of the long harpoon sometimes

25.text: has a small wooden or bone peg (Fig. 35, a, b), halfway of its

26.text: length, to allow a firmer grasp of the hand in throwing the

27.text: weapon. The shaft of the short harpoon is about four feet and

28.text: a half long; that of the long harpoon, eight feet and a half long.

29.text: The short harpoon is used in winter for killing seals through

30.text: their breathing-holes. These holes are found on the land-ice, or

31.text: on the floe nearest to the shore, whither the ringed and the

32.text: spotted seals resort in the winter time. The holes are concealed,

33.text: for the most part, under small snow mounds, and can be located

34.text: only with the aid of a keen-scented dog selected from the team

35.text: for the purpose. When the hole is found, the sealer sits down

36.text: to wait patiently, sometimes for hours. He brings along a small

37.text: wooden stool to sit on, or makes himself a seat of square pieces

38.text: of snow piled together, covering the top with a piece of reindeer-

39.text: skin. Another piece of skin he lays under his feet to keep the cold from his

40.text: soles. He gets the harpoon ready, frees the coil from the sinew twisting, and

41.text: lays it on his lap. If the snow covering of the hole is very thick, he cautiously

42.text: removes a portion of the snow. As soon as the seal is heard blowing, the

43.text: hunter suddenly stands up and throws the harpoon straight down into the hole
